title: Evaluating ideas in texts

draft.title: Evaluating ideas in texts
card: Evaluating an idea means judging how well a text supports it. A reader does not just accept a claim because it sounds confident.
ask what supports the claim. Facts, examples and data from a trusted source make a claim stronger. A claim with no support, or only the writer's opinion, is weaker.
ask what has been left out. A text may show only one side, or leave out facts that point the other way. This can make an idea seem stronger than it is.
A reader can then decide whether to accept the idea, doubt it, or look for more information.
draft.remember: Test an idea by asking what supports it and what is missing.

a.q: A blog says, "Everyone knows homework is useless." What is the best question for a reader to ask about this claim?
opts: What evidence shows that homework is useless?
How many words does the blog post use?
Who wrote the blog post's title?
Is the writer's opinion strongly stated?
a.why: Evaluating an idea means checking what supports it. The blog gives no evidence, only a confident statement. A strongly stated opinion is not a reason to accept a claim.
a.clue: Which question checks what backs up the claim?

b.q: An advert says, "Nine out of ten surveyed customers love Zing juice." It does not say how many were surveyed or who they were. What is the main weakness?
opts: Information about the evidence has been left out
The advert uses a number instead of a story
The advert is written to persuade customers
The claim is about what people like, not facts
b.why: Without the size and makeup of the survey, a reader cannot judge whether the result can be trusted. Using a number is not a weakness, and many texts persuade while still giving good evidence.
b.clue: Think about what the reader needs to know but is not told.

a.best: What evidence shows that homework is useless?

b.best: Information about the evidence has been left out
